source_propositions.source_text: The Syrian Army has assumed control of the al-Shaddadi military base in northeastern Syria’s Hasakah province, following coordination with U.S. officials, according to the Syrian Defense Ministry’s media department.
In a statement carried by Syrian Arab News Agency, the ministry said the base was formally handed over after arrangements were completed with U.S. authorities.
Syrian army units have since moved to secure the facility and its surrounding perimeter.
The transfer comes just days after Damascus announced it had taken control of the al-Tanf military base in southeastern Syria.
On February 12, the Defense Ministry said the handover of al-Tanf followed direct coordination between Syrian and American officials, marking a significant shift in the military presence in the area.
United States Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed its withdrawal from al-Tanf after nearly a decade of operations there.

In a statement, CENTCOM said U.S. forces remain prepared to respond to any potential threats from ISIS and will continue supporting partner-led efforts aimed at preventing the group’s resurgence in the region.
(ILKHA) LEGAL WARNING: All rights of the published news, photos and videos are reserved by İlke Haber Ajansı Basın Yayın San.

Eight people, including two children, were killed in a mass shooting at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday, while the suspected gunman also died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, bringing the total death toll to nine, authorities said.

A Russian strike on the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed at least 11 people, including three children, and wounded at least 16 others on Saturday, Oct. 10, local authorities said, as Russia launched a large-scale overnight drone attack across Ukraine.
İlke Haber Ajansı Basın Yayın Sanayi Ticaret A.Ş.
Alternative text - include a link to the PDF!
The move, in coordination with the US, is the latest implementation of the ceasefire agreement with Kurdish-led forces.

Syrian army takes control of al-Shaddadi base in coordination with US after its forces withdrew The Syrian army has taken over a military base in the northeast of the country following the withdrawal of United States troops, as part of a ceasefire deal with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).

Syria’s Ministry of Defence announced on Sunday that “forces of the Syrian Arab Army have taken over the al-Shaddadi military base in the Hasakah countryside following coordination with the American side”.
The US had been operating in al-Shadaddi since 2016, when the Kurdish-led forces seized it from ISIL (ISIS).

The US military and the SDF partnered in the fight against ISIL, but after the toppling of Syria’s longtime ruler, Bashar al-Assad, in 2024, Washington has backed interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa in his bid to impose control over the entire country.
The US helped broker the deal between al-Sharaa’s government and the SDF in January, after a dispute over the integration of the Kurdish-led forces into the Syrian army erupted into armed clashes.

source_propositions.source_text: Chip Thomas, a retired physician on the Navajo Reservation, is well known for his large photograhpic murals.
Now, he's been recognized with a MacArthur "genius" grant.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST: Think of street art and what might come to mind is city buildings with giant murals, subway cars tagged with spray paint or stenciled sidewalks.
Well, Chip Thomas creates street art in rural places - large-scale photographs on abandoned buildings across the Navajo Nation.
This year, the MacArthur Foundation gave Chip Thomas what's known as a genius grant.
KSUT's Adam Burke has this profile.
ADAM BURKE, BYLINE: North of Flagstaff, Arizona, the ribbon of highway disappears into a sea of sagebrush and yellow grasses.
THOMAS: My images of Kee John, who died at a young age from a cancer related to his work in a uranium mine. She's 29 and first started seeing Thomas' artwork as a teenager.
BURKE: At first, Thomas worked in secret too.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.
Chip Thomas is a public artist whose works are mostly located on the Navajo Nation and made in collaboration with Diné communities.
Thomas began this artistic work during a 36-year career as a primary care physician on the Navajo Nation.
Since 2009, Thomas has installed large black-and-white photographs on abandoned buildings, grain silos, and roadside structures across the Navajo Nation.
The photographs portray Diné people, animals, and landscapes, turning neglected structures into places of cultural memory and affirmation.
Some of Thomas's work addresses colonial violence and environmental damage, including the continuing health effects of abandoned uranium mines on Diné families.
The MacArthur Foundation selected 20 fellows in its 2026 class, including Chip Thomas.
Each 2026 fellow receives $800,000 over five years to use as they choose.
The selection process considers recommendations over several years; people do not apply for the fellowship.
